title: Human rights before and after Brexit
subtitle: Three regimes compared: the EU Charter, retained general principles, and the ECHR/Human Rights Act route
objectives: Explain why the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights stopped applying in UK domestic law at exit, and distinguish this from the separate survival of the ECHR
Describe how the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 narrowed the domestic effect of retained general principles of EU law, including rights-related ones

Correctly place a given human rights argument within the right regime — EU Charter (now defunct domestically), retained general principles (narrowed), or the ECHR/Human Rights Act (the surviving, functioning route) — without duplicating Public law's or Human rights law's treatment of the HRA itself

leadingAuthorities.role: Provides that the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights is not part of domestic law after exit, and constrains reliance on rights derived from it

leadingAuthorities.citation: Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 s 4
leadingAuthorities.role: Ends the general domestic effect of retained general principles of EU law (including rights-related principles) from 1 January 2024, subject to limited exceptions
Cross-reference only — the surviving, independent domestic mechanism for enforcing ECHR rights, taught in full elsewhere

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students often assume 'human rights law' is one undifferentiated thing that Brexit simply left alone because it 'isn't EU law'. This lesson exists because that assumption is half right and half dangerously wrong — some rights protection really did leave with EU membership, and some didn't move at all.

profileHooks.weakApplication: The test pool leans on sorting a rights-based argument into the correct one of three regimes. Read the comparison table in Part 4 twice before attempting those items — the regimes look similar on the surface but behave very differently.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with why the Charter and the ECHR are different instruments entirely, from different organisations, before anything about Brexit. That single distinction is the foundation the rest of this lesson builds on.

overview.hook: Three different bodies of law have, at different times, been called on to protect the same kind of claim — that a person's fundamental rights have been infringed. One of them vanished from UK law overnight at the end of the Brexit transition period. One of them was quietly narrowed by statute in 2024. One of them was never touched by Brexit at all and is still doing exactly the job it always did. Most students can name only the last one. This lesson is about not confusing the other two with it — or with each other.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 1 September 2026. The EU Charter and the narrowing of retained general principles are settled, concluded changes — not live negotiations. This lesson deliberately does not re-teach the mechanics of the Human Rights Act 1998 (ss 2, 3, 4, 6, 19) or the qualified-rights case law covered in Public law's dedicated HRA lesson and, where a student has taken it, the Human rights law module — it cross-references that material rather than duplicating it.

parts.heading: Three regimes, three origins — before any Brexit question arises
parts.voice: comparative — lays out the map before touching the politics
body: Before asking what Brexit changed, get the starting map straight, because the three regimes this lesson compares come from entirely different places and would be distinct even if the UK had never joined the EU. The European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) is a Council of Europe treaty, administered by the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg — an organisation with no institutional connection to the EU. It has applied to the UK since 1953 and is given further domestic effect by the Human Rights Act 1998, entirely untouched by Brexit.

The EU Charter of Fundamental Rights is a different document from a different organisation: it codifies rights recognised within EU law specifically, was given binding status by the Lisbon Treaty in 2009, and applied in UK law only because and only for as long as the UK was applying EU law generally — it was never an independent, freestanding source of rights protection in the way the ECHR is.

Retained general principles of EU law are a third, less visible thing again: broader principles the Court of Justice of the EU had developed over decades of EU-law adjudication — proportionality, legal certainty, equal treatment, and others with clear rights-flavoured content — which UK courts absorbed as part of EU membership and which the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 initially preserved in domestic law as 'retained EU law', separately from the Charter itself.

Three sources, three institutional homes, three different relationships to EU membership. Keep them separate from the outset, because the next three parts show each one taking a completely different post-Brexit path.

components.definition: ECHR/HRA (Strasbourg-derived, always independent of EU membership, untouched by Brexit); EU Charter of Fundamental Rights (EU-derived, applied only via EU membership, ended at exit); retained general principles of EU law (EU-derived, absorbed into domestic law at exit, subsequently narrowed by the REUL Act 2023).

interaction.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes the ECHR from the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights?
interaction.scenarioA: The ECHR is a Council of Europe treaty enforced via the Human Rights Act, wholly independent of EU membership; the Charter is an EU instrument that applied in UK law only because of EU membership.
interaction.scenarioB: The ECHR and the Charter are the same instrument, simply enforced through two different UK statutes.
interaction.explanation: These are genuinely separate instruments from separate organisations. Confusing them is the single most common error this lesson exists to correct.

parts.heading: Why the Charter stopped applying at exit
parts.voice: comparative — explains a clean, deliberate cut-off
body: Because the Charter's domestic application was parasitic on EU membership — it applied only when and because UK courts were applying EU law generally — Parliament could and did switch it off cleanly at the point of exit, rather than leaving it to fade through case-by-case erosion.

The European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 does this directly. Section 5(4) provides that the Charter is not part of domestic law on or after exit day. Section 5(5) goes further, addressing the risk that Charter-derived rights might survive indirectly by being re-labelled as 'retained general principles': it clarifies that a right, freedom or principle recognised only because it's reflected in the Charter (rather than existing independently in the underlying EU case law) does not form part of retained domestic law either.

The practical effect is total and immediate rather than gradual: a litigant cannot invoke the Charter, as such, in a UK court for anything happening after exit day, however similar their argument might have looked to a pre-exit Charter claim. This is the cleanest of the three post-Brexit transitions this lesson covers — an on/off switch, not a dimmer.

components.text: The Charter of Fundamental Rights is not part of domestic law on or after exit day. ... any right, power, liability, obligation, restriction, remedy or procedure which, immediately before exit day, is recognised and available in domestic law by virtue of section 2(1) of the European Communities Act 1972 (and would still be so recognised and available if the Charter of Fundamental Rights were not part of domestic law) continues on and after exit day to be recognised and available in domestic law ... but is not to be regarded as within subsection (4) merely because it is reflected in the Charter.
elements: The Charter itself is excluded from domestic law from exit day
A right existing independently in the underlying case law survives (as a retained general principle, subject to later REUL Act changes)
A right that exists only because the Charter reflects it does not survive merely by virtue of that reflection

interaction.prompt: Under s 5(4)-(5) EUWA 2018, if a right existed in the underlying pre-exit EU case law independently of the Charter (and was also reflected in the Charter), what is its post-exit status?
options: It could potentially continue as a retained general principle, because its survival doesn't depend merely on Charter reflection
It is automatically excluded from domestic law, because it is connected to the Charter at all
It survives only if expressly re-enacted by a new UK statute

parts.heading: The quieter change: narrowing retained general principles
parts.voice: comparative — a second, later and less total cut, contrasted with the Charter's total one
body: Retained general principles took a different path from the Charter, and it's worth being precise about the timeline: they survived exit day in 2020, continuing to have domestic effect as 'retained EU law' — and were only narrowed later, by a separate piece of legislation.

The Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023, in force from 1 January 2024, ends the general domestic effect of retained general principles of EU law. Section 4 provides that, from that date, no general principle of EU law is part of domestic law, and courts are no longer required (subject to specified exceptions) to interpret retained domestic legislation consistently with such principles or to disapply legislation for inconsistency with them. Proportionality-style arguments, equal treatment arguments and similar rights-flavoured claims that had previously been available through this route lost that particular avenue.

Contrast this with the Charter's clean 2020 cut-off: the general principles route survived for over three years after exit before being narrowed, and the REUL Act's language is about ending their 'general' domestic effect, with limited saved exceptions — a more surgical, later intervention than the Charter's blanket exclusion. A student who treats 'the Charter left at Brexit' and 'general principles left at Brexit' as the same event, at the same time, for the same reason, is wrong on both the date and the mechanism.

components.label: Charter vs general principles — the cut-off compared
points: Charter: excluded from domestic law from exit day (2020), by EUWA 2018 s 5(4)-(5) — total and immediate
General principles: initially preserved as retained EU law at exit, then narrowed later by REUL Act 2023 s 4, effective 1 January 2024
Different statutes, different dates, different mechanisms — do not conflate them
Both changes are settled, concluded law as at this lesson's check date, not live negotiation

interaction.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.
items: EU Charter of Fundamental Rights is excluded from UK domestic law at exit day, under EUWA 2018 s 5(4)-(5)
Retained general principles of EU law continue to have domestic effect as retained EU law after exit day
Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 receives Royal Assent
REUL Act 2023 s 4 ends the general domestic effect of retained general principles from 1 January 2024
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — the Charter's exclusion and the general principles' narrowing are separated by over three years and by two entirely different statutes.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the dates again — the Charter left domestic law at exit in 2020; general principles survived until the REUL Act narrowed them from 1 January 2024, more than three years later.

parts.heading: The route that never moved: ECHR and the Human Rights Act
parts.voice: comparative — deliberately brief, and explicit about not re-teaching material covered elsewhere
body: Against the Charter's total exclusion and the general principles' later narrowing, the third regime is defined by what didn't happen to it: nothing. The ECHR's status as a treaty the UK has ratified, and the Human Rights Act 1998's mechanism for giving Convention rights further domestic effect, were never EU law questions in the first place, and Brexit legislation makes no change to either.

This lesson deliberately does not re-teach how the Human Rights Act works — the interpretive obligation under s 3, declarations of incompatibility under s 4, the meaning of 'public authority' under s 6, or the qualified-rights proportionality structure. That is Public law's dedicated HRA lesson, and — for a student who has taken it — the Human rights law module goes considerably further into individual Convention articles. This lesson's job is narrower: to make sure a student doesn't wrongly assume the HRA route was affected by Brexit at all, or confuse a live ECHR-based argument with a now-unavailable Charter-based one.

The practical consequence for an exam answer: if a fact pattern raises a genuine human rights concern today, the ECHR/HRA route is very likely still the live one to reach for — subject to whatever that lesson's own limits and exceptions are — while a Charter-based argument is available only for events that occurred before exit day, and a general-principles argument is now available only within REUL Act 2023's narrower saved exceptions.

components.title: Which regime does a rights-based argument belong to?
components.description: A decision path for classifying a rights-flavoured claim after Brexit.

nodes.label: Is the claim based on a Convention right (e.g. Article 8 privacy, Article 6 fair trial)?
Yes → ECHR/HRA route — unaffected by Brexit; see Public law's HRA lesson / Human rights law module
No → is the claim based specifically on the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights?
Yes → excluded from domestic law from exit day (EUWA 2018 s 5(4)); only relevant to pre-exit events
No → is the claim based on a general principle of EU law (e.g. proportionality, equal treatment) developed in CJEU case law?
Yes → check REUL Act 2023 s 4's narrow saved exceptions; general effect ended from 1 January 2024
No → not one of these three regimes; consider ordinary domestic public law or common law grounds

components.textAlternative: First ask if the claim is based on a Convention right — if so, it's the ECHR/HRA route, unaffected by Brexit and covered elsewhere. If not, ask if it's based specifically on the EU Charter — if so, it was excluded from domestic law at exit day and is only relevant to pre-exit events. If not, ask if it's based on a general principle of EU law developed in CJEU case law — if so, check the REUL Act 2023's narrow saved exceptions, since general effect ended from 1 January 2024. If none of these apply, it isn't one of these three regimes at all.

interaction.prompt: A claimant argues that a 2026 UK government decision breached their Article 8 ECHR right to respect for private life. Which regime governs this claim, and is it affected by Brexit?
options: The ECHR/Human Rights Act route — unaffected by Brexit, since it was never dependent on EU membership
The EU Charter route — excluded from domestic law and therefore unavailable
Retained general principles — narrowed by the REUL Act 2023 and therefore unavailable
interaction.explanation: An Article 8 ECHR argument engages the Human Rights Act route, which is entirely untouched by Brexit. It is neither the (now-excluded) Charter nor a (narrowed) general principle.

parts.heading: Putting the map to work: sorting arguments by regime
parts.voice: comparative — closes with contrastive practice across all three regimes at once
body: With the map complete, the remaining skill is speed and accuracy in sorting a rights-flavoured argument into the right box before analysing it substantively — because starting an answer in the wrong regime wastes time and can lead you to apply a mechanism (like s 3 HRA interpretation, or Charter disapplication) that simply isn't available for that argument any more.

A useful discipline: ask first which organisation or instrument the argument traces back to. 'Strasbourg' or 'Convention' language points to the ECHR/HRA route. 'Charter of Fundamental Rights' or 'EU Charter' language points to the now-excluded Charter route, relevant only pre-exit. Language about a 'general principle of EU law' — proportionality in the EU-law sense, legal certainty, equal treatment as developed by the CJEU — points to the narrowed general-principles route, and you should immediately ask whether the specific principle falls within one of the REUL Act's saved exceptions.

This is also the natural point to note what this lesson deliberately leaves for elsewhere: the substantive content of Convention rights, the mechanics of ss 2–4 and 6 HRA, and current debates about reforming or replacing the HRA are all covered — in more depth than this lesson could or should attempt — in Public law's HRA lesson and, for a student taking it, the dedicated Human rights law module. This lesson's contribution is the map, not the destination.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students sometimes write that 'human rights protection ended when the UK left the EU', treating the loss of the Charter as if it were the loss of human rights protection generally.
components.whyItsWrong: This conflates a narrow, EU-specific instrument (the Charter, genuinely excluded) with the much broader and entirely unaffected ECHR/HRA system, which remains the primary domestic mechanism for human rights claims. The accurate statement is that one of three regimes was switched off, one was narrowed, and one was never touched.

interaction.prompt: Which of these best captures the overall post-Brexit picture across the three regimes discussed in this lesson?
options: Human rights protection in UK law ended entirely at Brexit
The EU Charter was excluded at exit, retained general principles were later narrowed by the REUL Act 2023, and the ECHR/Human Rights Act route was unaffected throughout
All three regimes were abolished at the same time by the same statute
interaction.trapExplanation: The tempting simplification treats Brexit as ending 'human rights law' as a single block. The accurate picture requires holding three separate, differently-timed developments in mind at once.

testPool.prompt: Which UK statute provides that the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights is not part of domestic law on or after exit day?
Is the European Convention on Human Rights an EU instrument?
options: No — it is a Council of Europe treaty, unconnected institutionally to the EU
Yes — it is one of the EU's founding treaties

testPool.prompt: Which Act narrows the domestic effect of retained general principles of EU law from 1 January 2024?
options: Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023
European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018

testPool.prompt: Which statement correctly compares the timing of the Charter's exclusion and the narrowing of general principles?
options: Both happened simultaneously at exit day in 2020
The Charter was excluded at exit day (2020); general principles were narrowed later, from 1 January 2024, by a separate statute
General principles were narrowed first, and the Charter was excluded afterwards
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to bundle these as one 'Brexit ended EU rights protection' event — they are in fact separated by more than three years and enacted by two different statutes.

testPool.prompt: Under EUWA 2018 s 5(5), a right that exists only because it is reflected in the Charter (with no independent basis in the underlying case law) has what post-exit status?
options: It does not form part of retained domestic law
It automatically becomes a retained general principle regardless of independent basis
It is preserved permanently by the Human Rights Act

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that most precisely states why the ECHR/HRA route was unaffected by Brexit.
testPool.passage: The European Convention on Human Rights is a Council of Europe treaty, administered by the European Court of Human Rights, with no institutional connection to the EU. Because the Human Rights Act 1998's mechanism for enforcing Convention rights domestically was never dependent on the UK's EU membership, Brexit legislation makes no change to it. This stands in contrast to the EU Charter, whose domestic application was entirely parasitic on that membership.
testPool.ratioSentence: Because the Human Rights Act 1998's mechanism for enforcing Convention rights domestically was never dependent on the UK's EU membership, Brexit legislation makes no change to it.

testPool.prompt: Which of these two claims is correctly classified?
testPool.scenarioA: 'A claimant relies on Article 3 ECHR (prohibition of torture) via the Human Rights Act — this route remains available post-Brexit.'
testPool.scenarioB: 'A claimant relies on Article 3 ECHR via the Human Rights Act — this route was excluded from domestic law at exit day along with the EU Charter.'
testPool.explanation: The ECHR/HRA route was never dependent on EU membership and was entirely unaffected by Brexit — B wrongly extends the Charter's exclusion to the separate ECHR/HRA regime.

testPool.prompt: A pre-2026 problem question describes an argument based on 'the EU-law general principle of proportionality as developed by the CJEU, with no separate basis in the ECHR'. Which response correctly applies this lesson?
testPool.scenarioA: Treat the argument as automatically available in full, since general principles were preserved as retained EU law at exit and nothing has changed since.
testPool.scenarioB: Recognise that, from 1 January 2024, the REUL Act 2023 ended the general domestic effect of such principles, so the argument is now only available if it falls within one of the Act's specified saved exceptions.
testPool.explanation: Simply citing 'general principles survived exit' is out of date — the REUL Act 2023 narrowed their effect from 1 January 2024, and the current analysis must check for a saved exception rather than assume general availability.

testPool.prompt: A litigant in 2026 wants to argue that a UK regulatory decision breaches 'the right to good administration' as it appears in the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, with no independent basis outside the Charter. Can this argument succeed on that basis alone?
options: No — the Charter is not part of domestic law from exit day, and a right with no independent basis outside the Charter does not survive merely because it is reflected there
Yes — the Charter continues to apply in full to all post-exit decisions
Yes, but only if the decision-maker is a public authority under the Human Rights Act
testPool.explanation: This is squarely EUWA 2018 s 5(4)-(5): the Charter itself is excluded, and a right that exists only by virtue of Charter reflection (with no independent basis) does not survive that exclusion.

testPool.prompt: A claimant in 2026 argues their treatment by a public authority breached Article 6 ECHR (fair trial). Should this argument be analysed using the EU Charter framework, the retained general principles framework, or the Human Rights Act framework?
options: The Human Rights Act framework — this is a Convention rights claim, unrelated to either EU-derived regime
The EU Charter framework, since Article 6 ECHR has an equivalent Charter article
The retained general principles framework, since fair trial rights were also a CJEU-developed general principle
testPool.explanation: The claim is framed as an ECHR right. Even though the Charter and general principles both historically touched on similar ideas (like fair trial protections), an Article 6 ECHR claim belongs in the HRA framework — covered in depth elsewhere, not re-taught here.

testPool.prompt: A litigant has a rights-based argument and needs to work out which framework applies. Put these diagnostic steps in the right order.
items: Ask whether the argument is based on a Convention (ECHR) right
If not, ask whether it is based specifically on the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights
If not, ask whether it is based on a general principle of EU law developed in CJEU case law
Apply the correct regime's current post-Brexit status to determine whether the argument is available

testPool.prompt: A claimant challenges a 2026 UK government decision on two grounds: (1) that it breaches Article 8 ECHR, and (2) that it breaches the EU Charter's right to protection of personal data, relying solely on the Charter with no independent basis in retained general principles. Analyse the current availability of each ground.
factsToOrder: Ground (1) is framed as an ECHR/Human Rights Act claim
Ground (2) is framed solely as an EU Charter claim, with no independent basis
EUWA 2018 s 5(4) excludes the Charter from domestic law from exit day
The Human Rights Act was never affected by Brexit legislation

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether each of the two grounds is currently available as at 2026, given their different regimes.
modelAnswer.rule: ECHR/HRA claims are unaffected by Brexit. EU Charter claims are excluded from domestic law from exit day under EUWA 2018 s 5(4), and a right with no independent basis outside the Charter does not survive merely by virtue of Charter reflection (s 5(5)).
modelAnswer.application: Ground (1) is a straightforward Convention rights claim under the Human Rights Act, a route never touched by Brexit legislation — it remains available in principle (subject to the ordinary HRA framework taught elsewhere). Ground (2) relies solely on the Charter with no independent basis; since the Charter itself is excluded from domestic law and this right has no separate existence outside it, s 5(4)-(5) removes this ground.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Ground (1) remains available under the HRA framework. Ground (2) is not available, because it depends entirely on the now-excluded EU Charter with no independent surviving basis.

testPool.prompt: Why is it a mistake to say 'the UK left the EU, so it left human rights protection'?
options: Because it conflates the EU-specific Charter (genuinely excluded) and narrowed general principles with the ECHR/Human Rights Act system, which is institutionally separate from the EU and entirely unaffected by Brexit
Because the statement is correct and there is no mistake
Because the ECHR was also abolished by the REUL Act 2023
testPool.trapExplanation: The instinct to treat 'EU' and 'human rights law' as synonymous is the exact error this lesson targets — the ECHR/HRA system predates and stands entirely apart from EU membership.

testPool.prompt: How confident should a student be that the Human Rights Act's mechanics (ss 2, 3, 4, 6, 19) are covered in depth within this EU law lesson, rather than cross-referenced to Public law and Human rights law?
sliderLabels: Not confident — this lesson deliberately cross-references rather than re-teaches those mechanics
Fully confident — this lesson is the primary source for HRA mechanics
testPool.explanation: This lesson is explicit that HRA mechanics are covered elsewhere (Public law's HRA lesson, and the Human rights law module where taken) — its own job is limited to mapping which regime a rights argument belongs to.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating the three regimes as a single block that 'ended with Brexit'. In fact each has a distinct status: the Charter was excluded outright at exit, general principles were narrowed later and only partially, and the ECHR/HRA route was never affected at all. Sorting a given argument into the correct one of the three, with the correct timing, is the tested skill.
